clue.text: Mould old aviator after number one is dropped

indicators.note: after places the trimmed aviator behind the abbreviation for number
is dropped says the letter for one falls out of the aviator's surname

parts.note: Louis Blériot, the French pioneer who first flew the Channel in 1909
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A story of a forgotten pilot going mouldy once the leading figure has fallen away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' looks like a single phrase, but 'number' gives NO and 'one' is the I taken from BLERIOT, leaving BLEROT.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a grey fungus on ripening grapes, prized by makers of sweet dessert wines such as Sauternes.

clue.text: One who served for his country died crashing into European mountain

definitions.text: One who served for his country

indicators.note: crashing into says the letter for died breaks inside the European mountain

parts.note: berg is a mountain, as in iceberg or the German word
D is the genealogical abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A soldier who served his nation is killed when his plane crashes into an Alpine peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served' suggests military service, but this is tennis: Stefan Edberg, the Swedish player famous for serve and volley.
explanation.definitionFit: Stefan Edberg was a Swedish tennis champion who served in Davis Cup ties representing Sweden.

clue.text: Having an air of protest, bubbly Rachel loves to interrupt most of females

indicators.note: to interrupt says the shuffled name and verb break into the shortened females
most of says the word for females loses its final letter

parts.note: women are females

indicators.note: bubbly means effervescent, so the letters of Rachel loves fizz into a new order

explanation.surface: A cheerful Rachel, with a protesting manner, enjoys butting in on a group of women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' is a tune here, not an attitude; 'Having' is only a link. 'bubbly' signals the anagram and 'to interrupt' the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: The gospel-derived anthem became the signature song of the US civil rights movement, so it is a tune of protest.

clue.text: Quick bite? Lunch organised

definitions.note: quick in its old sense means pregnant, as in quick with child

indicators.note: organised means arranged, so the letters of bite and lunch are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A snack eaten in a hurry: a lunch thrown together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick bite' reads as a hasty snack, but 'Quick' is the definition, in its archaic sense of pregnant, and 'bite' joins LUNCH as anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are expressions for being pregnant; quick in this old sense means carrying a child that has started to move.

clue.text: During study, trainee's first recess

parts.note: in means during, as in in the night
a den is a private room for work, a study

indicators.note: first says only the opening letter of trainee's is used

explanation.surface: While at his desk, the trainee takes his first break.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess is a set-back notch or hollow in an edge or surface, just like a dent cut into it.

clue.text: Also, grub is served up around one in such a style?

indicators.note: around says the reversed dig word wraps round the word for also
is served up says, in a down clue, that the word for grub is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to grub is to dig or root about
and means also, in addition
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Food served up in a particular manner, which the question mark invites you to guess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grub' is the verb dig, not food. The question mark flags that the definition is a hint at the clay-oven cooking style.
explanation.definitionFit: Food cooked in a clay oven is described by this adjective, so it names a manner of cooking.

clue.text: Household device for re-heating kippers

parts.note: kippers are smoked fish, but here they are people having a kip, that is sleepers, warmed in bed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kippers' suggests smoked herring warmed in a pan; read as people taking a kip, they are sleepers being warmed in bed. Kip is British slang for sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: This mains-powered bedcover heats the bed, and so warms whoever is asleep in it.

clue.text: Old Bolshevik pressing Eastern church to show mercy

indicators.note: pressing means squeezing, so the revolutionary's name hugs the letter for Eastern

parts.note: Lenin led the Bolshevik revolution
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A Soviet revolutionary leans on an Orthodox church to be merciful.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lenient means showing mildness and clemency instead of severity, which is mercy.

clue.text: British command having the edge

parts.note: an order is a command

explanation.surface: A British instruction that gives somebody an advantage over a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the edge' reads as having an advantage; 'edge' alone is the definition, a margin or rim.
explanation.definitionFit: A margin or boundary strip running round something is its edge.

clue.text: Former head, a classy chap

parts.note: old means former, as in an old flame
bean is informal slang for the head

explanation.surface: An ex-headmaster, a refined fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a dated, upper-class British form of address for a friend, so it names a posh fellow.

clue.text: Screw undone, ergo almost out

definitions.note: screw is prison slang for a warder

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged
almost says the last letter of ergo is dropped

explanation.surface: A loose screw has come undone, so it is nearly out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' looks like hardware; it is prison slang for a jailer. 'almost' trims ERGO to ERG, and 'out' rearranges UNDONE ERG.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in charge of a dungeon is a jailer, and a prison officer is called a screw in slang.

clue.text: Parasite taking skin off edible fruit

parts.note: a leech is a blood-sucking parasite

indicators.note: skin off means the outer layer of edible, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A bloodsucker peels the skin from a piece of fruit you can eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skin off' might suggest removing the outside letters, but here it means taking them: the E and E that skin edible.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a variant spelling of lychee, the Chinese fruit with white flesh under a rough shell.

clue.text: Jester extremely irritating in part — too much backtracking

indicators.note: in puts the edge letters inside the word for part

parts.note: a role is a part in a play

indicators.note: extremely means taking the extremes, the first and last letters of irritating
backtracking says the over-the-top abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top, too much

explanation.surface: A court fool who is extremely irritating in his role, going back and overdoing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives IG from irritating, which goes into ROLE; 'backtracking' reverses OTT to TTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's opera is named after its title character, the hunchbacked court jester to the Duke of Mantua.

clue.text: Service break

parts.note: service suggests tennis, where breaking serve wins a game, but this is leave from military service

explanation.walkthrough: 'Service break' sounds like tennis, a broken serve; it is time off from the armed services.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation stands for rest and recreation, the leave given to troops away from duty.

clue.text: There's no danger Catholics will mess with Teresa

indicators.note: mess with means tamper with, so the letters of Catholics and Teresa are jumbled together

explanation.surface: Reassurance that the faithful will cause Teresa no harm by meddling in her affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from smugglers watching for coastguards, means that nobody is watching and it is safe to proceed.

clue.text: Noise-suppression device connected to organs

parts.note: the organs are hearing ones, and the device is a pair of warm pads joined over them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs' suggests church organs drowning out noise; the organs are those on either side of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: These padded coverings worn over the ears keep out cold and also muffle sound.

clue.text: Band maintaining safety in an estate, say

definitions.text: Band maintaining safety in an estate, say

parts.words: Band maintaining safety in an estate, say
parts.note: an estate here is a British estate car, a station wagon, and the band is the strap that keeps a passenger secure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Estate' suggests a country property with guards; in Britain an estate is a station wagon, one example of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The strap across a car passenger's body is a band that keeps the person safe in a crash.

clue.text: Animals toned up in fresh air

indicators.note: in puts the reworked toned inside the reworked air
fresh means new, so the letters of air take a new order
up means stirred up, so the letters of toned are rearranged

explanation.surface: Creatures getting fit while exercising outdoors in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads as a fitness word with 'toned', but it is a second anagram signal alongside 'fresh'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the zoological order of gnawing mammals such as rats, mice and squirrels.

clue.text: Magical female left out of group

indicators.note: out of says the letter for left is removed from the word for group

parts.note: a circle is a group, as in a circle of friends

explanation.surface: A witch left out of a social set.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer's Odyssey she is the sorceress who turns Odysseus's crew into swine.

clue.text: Pass on porky dog

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
porky is short for porky pie, Cockney rhyming slang for a lie

explanation.surface: Skip feeding the fat dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porky' is Cockney rhyming slang: porky pie rhymes with lie.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a breed of sheepdog originating in Scotland.

clue.text: Fused lead taking yonks to melt

indicators.note: to melt means to become liquid and lose shape, so the letters of lead and yonks are remade

explanation.surface: Fused metal: the lead takes ages to melt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yonks' is British slang for a very long time.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical term describes joints or bones that have grown together and stiffened, which is fused.

clue.text: Light touch applied to hem of madame's veil

indicators.note: applied to joins the gentle touch on to the edge letters

parts.note: a kiss is a gentle touch, as of a breeze or the lips

indicators.note: hem of means the edge of madame, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A gentle touch of the hand to the hem of a lady's veil.
explanation.definitionFit: In old dress this was a name for a short veil or a small bonnet, an inviting piece of headwear.

clue.text: Look to Italy to welcome France

indicators.note: welcome means take in, so the closed word holds the letter for France

parts.note: to means shut, as when a door is pushed to
F is the international vehicle code for France
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A message to look to Italy to host France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcome' puts F inside SHUT, giving SHUFT, before I. 'to' reads as a link but means closed, as a door pushed to.
explanation.definitionFit: This slang term, from Arabic and spread by British soldiers, means a quick glance.

clue.text: Boy, caught by stream, a source of irritation

indicators.note: caught as in heard, so the word for boy is taken by ear

parts.note: a son is a boy
a burn is a stream in Scotland and northern England

explanation.surface: A lad, trapped by a river, finds something that gets on his nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' looks like C or a containment signal; here it means heard.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin reddened by too much exposure to sunlight is sore and itchy, so it is one cause of irritation.

clue.text: Remains found in sinister elements of test?

parts.note: sinister is Latin for left, as in heraldry
a Test match in cricket is made of overs, sets of six balls bowled

explanation.surface: Remains discovered in the darkest parts of a medical test.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match, and an over is a set of six deliveries from one end.
explanation.definitionFit: Food uneaten after a meal, or anything still around afterwards, is what remains.

clue.text: Masters' shirt seams partly turned back

indicators.note: turned back says the hidden letters are read backwards
partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Tailors inspect the seams of their bosses' shirts after turning them back.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian plural of maestro, used for great musicians or conductors, means masters of their art.

clue.text: Enclose article on ambassador stopping WWII entertainers

indicators.note: on says the article is placed after the entertainers in this across answer
stopping means plugging a gap, so the envoy's title sits inside the entertainers

parts.note: ENSA, the Entertainments National Service Association, put on shows for British troops in the Second World War
HE is His Excellency, the title of an ambassador
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: An article about a diplomat who halts a troupe of wartime entertainers.
explanation.walkthrough: ENSA was the British organisation that staged shows for troops in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: To put into a sheath or covering is to enclose something completely.
